name: Mixcloud
subcategory: DJ mix and radio show hosting
tagline: Hosting and streaming for DJ mixes, radio shows and long-form audio, with licensing built in.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The technical part of Mixcloud is a weekend project: store big audio files, transcode to HLS, stream them, show a waveform and a tracklist. The part you cannot build is the reason DJs use it at all, which is that Mixcloud has royalty arrangements with rights bodies so a two hour mix of other people's records can sit online without getting pulled. Self-host the same mix and you are personally the one receiving the takedown, or worse. On top of that there is the audience: people browse Mixcloud, follow shows, and get recommended mixes, and none of that exists on a box you own. A private archive of your own sets is a fine build, a public mix platform is not.
coreLoopDIY: A self-hosted archive that ingests long audio files, transcodes them for streaming, and plays them back with a waveform and timestamped tracklist.
requirements: Local machine or small VPS with real disk space
Object storage or a big volume if you have more than a few dozen mixes
Your own answer on music licensing if anything is public
whatYouLose: Licensing cover, which is the actual product: your self-hosted mixes are your legal problem
Listeners, follows, and the discovery feed that brings new people to a show
Mixcloud Select and the fan subscription plumbing that monetizes an audience
Native apps plus car, Sonos and TV playback that people already have installed
Bandwidth and CDN economics for streaming hour-long files to strangers
moatNotes: Rights deals are the whole business model. Everything else is a media server.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a DJ posting a mix wants two things: for it to stay up, and for someone to hear it. Mixcloud sells both, and neither is code. The royalty arrangements mean a mix full of commercial tracks does not vanish in a week, and the platform's own traffic means uploading is also distribution. A Pro subscription buys longer uploads, better stats and download options on top of that base, but the base is the point. A self-hosted clone gives you storage you were already paying for and an audience of zero.
notes: Build this for your own archive, not as a public platform. The moat is not the player, it is the rights clearance that keeps other people's music legally streamable.
prompt:
Build a self-hosted personal mix archive: a private web app for storing and streaming my own long-form DJ mixes and radio shows.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Next.js 15 with the App Router and TypeScript
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, single file at ./data/archive.db
- Audio files on local disk under ./data/audio, served through a Next route handler that supports HTTP range requests
- ffmpeg shelled out from a Node script for transcoding, no cloud media APIs
- Tailwind for styling, wavesurfer.js for the waveform, no component library

Features in scope:
- Upload page accepting large audio files (mp3, m4a, flac, wav) with a resumable-ish chunked upload, up to 4 GB
- On upload, a background job transcodes to a 128 kbps HLS ladder plus a single progressive mp3, extracts duration, and generates a downsampled waveform peaks JSON file
- Mix detail page: waveform player with seek, play, keyboard space to toggle, remembered playback position in localStorage
- Timestamped tracklist editor: paste lines like "00:14:32 Artist - Title", parsed into rows, clicking a row seeks the player
- Library page: list of mixes with cover art, duration, date, tags, and a text search over title, notes and tracklist entries
- Edit page for title, description, cover image, tags, recorded date
- Optional public share link per mix: a random unguessable slug that renders a read-only player page, off by default

Explicitly out of scope: user accounts, a discovery feed, following, comments, recommendations, fan subscriptions, payments, analytics, telemetry, mobile apps, and anything touching music licensing. Single-user, single trusted machine.

Operational details:
- One command dev setup, npm run dev, and npm run ingest to batch import a folder of existing files
- Single optional env var ARCHIVE_PASSWORD in .env for basic auth on all non-share routes; if unset, no auth and say so in the README
- README covers the ffmpeg dependency, disk usage expectations, how to back up ./data, and a blunt note that publicly sharing mixes of copyrighted music is on me, not on this code
